methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective cohort study with propensity score matching to balance baseline characteristics; pre-specified endpoints (PFS, OS); appropriate statistical methods including Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank tests, Cox proportional hazards models, and network meta-analysis using fixed-effects models. Acknowledged limitations: single-center, non-randomized design, potential selection bias not fully addressed by PSM, missing PD-L1 data in 45.8% of cohort.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual cohort study addressing real-world practice question: does adding bevacizumab to first-line chemoimmunotherapy improve survival in EGFR/ALK-negative NSCLC? Findings (PFS improvement without OS benefit despite increased toxicity) are clinically relevant but highlight uncertainty rather than provide definitive guidance. No clear subgroup benefits identified on OS, limiting translational impact.

reporting_quality.justification: Cohort study appropriately adheres to STROBE reporting standard with detailed Methods, patient characteristics in Table 1, clearly reported outcomes with CIs and p-values, and explicit Limitations section acknowledging selection bias, retrospective AE collection, and missing biomarker data. However, no statement of data availability or code sharing; retrospective AE collection noted as potentially incomplete with underreporting in medical records.

novelty_literature.justification: Combines retrospective real-world cohort with network meta-analysis examining I+C+B vs I+C in EGFR/ALK-negative NSCLC, addressing a documented clinical gap. However, the main finding—PFS benefit without OS gain—largely confirms prior trial results (IMpower150, APPLE); subgroup analyses (age, brain metastases, PD-L1) offer incremental insights but no OS benefit in any subgroup limits novelty.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear structure: Introduction contextualizes prior trials effectively, Methods describe cohort eligibility and statistical approaches thoroughly, Results clearly present survival curves and subgroup findings, Discussion provides mechanistic interpretation. Figures support narrative well. Minor issues: some repetition between Results and Discussion; discussion of bevacizumab mechanisms somewhat lengthy relative to key findings.

key_strengths: Real-world data complement randomized trials, addressing practical clinical uncertainty about I+C+B benefit in EGFR/ALK-negative NSCLC
Dual approach combining propensity-matched cohort with network meta-analysis strengthens evidence synthesis
Clear reporting of both efficacy (PFS benefit) and safety trade-off (increased grade 3-5 AEs, fatal hemorrhage), supporting cautious clinical interpretation
Comprehensive subgroup analyses (PD-L1, age, metastatic sites, chemotherapy) examining differential treatment effects
Explicit acknowledgment of limitations including selection bias, missing biomarkers, and lack of OS benefit tempering interpretation
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with selection bias despite PSM; I+C+B cohort younger and more paclitaxel-exposed, suggesting inherent prognostic imbalance
Nearly 46% missing PD-L1 data limits power to identify biomarker-driven predictive subgroups; post-hoc subgroup analyses without multiple testing correction inflates Type I error
Key finding—PFS benefit without OS advantage—provides limited clinical guidance; authors appropriately conclude no clear benefit-risk threshold but this limits actionability
Modest sample size (n=277) and relatively short follow-up may mask subtle OS differences or later-emerging safety signals
No data or code availability statement; retrospective AE ascertainment acknowledged as incomplete, raising reproducibility concerns
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically competent real-world study addressing a genuine clinical gap with appropriate statistical approaches and transparent reporting of both benefits and harms. While the PFS-without-OS finding is clinically relevant, it is largely confirmatory of prior trials (IMpower150, APPLE) rather than paradigm-shifting. Suitable for Tier 2 (JIF 10-19) venue such as ESMO Open or JCO Precision Oncology given solid methodology and translational relevance, but incremental novelty and inconclusive clinical benefit preclude higher tier consideration.
